data:
Looking for AI agent integration? This page covers running AI models inside AD4M. If you want AI agents to use AD4M — creating perspectives, managing data, joining neighbourhoods — see the MCP Server guide.
AD4M provides powerful AI capabilities through both local and remote model inference. This allows you to integrate various AI models into your applications, from language models to embedding models and speech recognition.
data.overview#Overview:
The AI system in AD4M supports:
Large Language Models (LLM) for text generation and chat
Embedding Models for vector representations of text
Speech-to-Text Models for audio transcription
Both local and remote (API-based) model execution
Model management and configuration
Task-based inference with system prompts and examples
data.model-configuration#Model Configuration: Before using AI features, models need to be configured in the AD4M Launcher. Models can be either local (running on your device) or remote (using external APIs).
data.local-models#Local Models: Local models run directly on your device using CPU or GPU acceleration (if available). There are three ways to configure local models:
data.1-pre-configured-models#1. Pre-configure:
AD4M comes with several pre-configured models that can be used by simply specifying their name:
const preConfiguredModel = {
  name: "DeepHermes 3 (Q4)",
  local: {
    fileName: "deephermes-3-llama-3-8b-Q4"  // Just specify the model name
  },
  modelType: "LLM"
};
Available pre-configured models:Language Models (LLM):
Qwen2.5.1-Coder-7B-Instruct - Optimized for coding tasks
deephermes-3-llama-3-8b-Q4 - Fast, efficient 8B parameter model (Q4 quantization)
deephermes-3-llama-3-8b-Q6 - Better quality, slightly larger (Q6 quantization)
deephermes-3-llama-3-8b-Q8 - Best quality, largest size (Q8 quantization)
deepseek_r1_distill_qwen_1_5b - Small, fast 1.5B parameter model
deepseek_r1_distill_qwen_7b - Medium 7B parameter model
deepseek_r1_distill_qwen_14b - Large 14B parameter model
Embedding Models:
bert - Built-in BERT model for text embeddings
Speech-to-Text Models:
Whisper - OpenAI's Whisper model for audio transcription
data.hardware-acceleration#Hardware Accelerat:
AD4M automatically detects and uses available hardware acceleration:
CUDA: For NVIDIA GPUs (requires cuda feature)
Metal: For Apple Silicon and AMD GPUs on macOS (requires metal feature)
CPU: Falls back to CPU if no GPU acceleration is available
data.best-practices#Best Practices:
Model Selection
Use quantized models (Q4/Q6) for faster inference on CPU
Use larger models when quality is critical
Consider API models for production use cases
Task Design
Write clear system prompts
Provide specific examples
Use task-specific models when possible
Resource Management
Close transcription streams when done
Monitor model loading status
Handle errors appropriately
Performance
Use GPU acceleration when available
Batch similar requests together
Consider model size vs performance tradeoffs
data.model-updates#Model Updates:
Models can be updated while maintaining tasks:
const updated = await client.ai.updateModel(modelId, newConfig);
data.automatic-stream-cleanup#Automatic Strea:
Transcription streams are automatically cleaned up after 30 seconds of inactivity to prevent resource leaks. This means:
No need to manually close streams if the client disconnects
Resources are freed automatically when streams are abandoned
Streams remain active as long as they receive audio data regularly

data.overview#Overview: AD4M uses a capability-based security model to protect user data and control access to agent functionality. Every application that wants to interact with an AD4M executor needs to request specific capabilities, which are then granted (or denied) by the user.
data.what-are-capabilities#What are Capabilit:
Capabilities in AD4M are like permission tokens that:
Define what data an application can access (which perspectives)
Specify what operations an application can perform
Are scoped to specific domains and functions
Can be revoked by the user at any time
A capability token might grant permissions like:
Read access to specific perspectives
Write access to create or modify links
Ability to create new perspectives
Permission to manage agent relationships
Access to specific language functions
data.standard-flow#Standard Flow:
When an application wants to connect to an AD4M executor, it goes through a secure authentication handshake:
The application requests access with specific capabilities
The AD4M executor generates a random verification code
The user must confirm the request and enter the code
Upon successful verification, a capability token is issued
This flow ensures that:
The user explicitly approves application access
The application only gets the permissions it needs
The connection between UI and executor is secure
data.remote-multi-user-authentication#Remote:
When connecting to a remote multi-user host (with hosting: true set in
ad4m-connect), the user selects the Remote Node option on the connection screen
and then chooses or enters a host URL. After selecting a host, the authentication flow
differs from the local capability handshake described above.Instead of the code-based authorization dialog, ad4m-connect presents an email +
password form:
New users enter an email address and password to create an account. If the host has
SMTP configured, a verification code is sent to the email and must be entered to complete
registration.
Returning users enter their email and password to log in. With SMTP enabled, a
verification code is sent on each login for additional security.
Behind the scenes, this calls ad4m.agent.createUser() or
ad4m.agent.requestLoginVerification() / ad4m.agent.verifyEmailCode() as described in
the Multi-User Mode documentation.Each user receives their own DID and a scoped JWT token upon successful
authentication. The token is managed automatically by ad4m-connect for all subsequent
API calls.
Note: The remote authentication flow is shown when the user connects to a remote
host. The local capability handshake is shown when connecting to a local node.
ad4m-connect handles both flows — apps do not need to implement either one manually.
data.admin-credential-override#Admin Credenti:
For automated scenarios or system integration, the authentication handshake can be bypassed using an admin credential:
// In your application
const client = new Ad4mClient({
  adminCredential: "your-secret-here",
});
This is particularly useful for:
CI/CD pipelines
Testing environments
System services
Management interfaces (the AD4M Launcher uses this internally)
The executor requires one: ad4m-executor run exits with an error when no admin credential (or an empty one) is set. Pass it through the environment, not the command line:
export AD4M_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL="your-secret-here"
ad4m-executor run
For tests and local development, --insecure-no-admin-credential (or AD4M_INSECURE_NO_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL=true) starts the executor without a credential; an empty token then has full admin access on a loopback-bound API, and is anonymous on a network-bound one (--localhost false, or TLS).⚠️ Security Note: The admin credential grants full access to the executor. Use it carefully and never expose it in client-side code or public repositories.
data.best-practices#Best Practices:
Request Minimal Capabilities
Only request permissions your app actually needs
Use specific domains and operations instead of wildcards
Consider read-only access when possible
Handle Authentication States
Check if capabilities are still valid
Implement reconnection logic
Handle capability revocation gracefully
Secure Storage
Store capability tokens securely
Never expose admin credentials
Implement token refresh mechanisms
User Experience
Clearly explain why your app needs certain capabilities
Provide feedback during the authentication process
Handle errors gracefully
data.more-information#More Information:
For more details about implementing authentication in your application:
Check the ad4m-connect documentation
See the Ad4mClient API reference

data.overview#Overview: Batch operations in AD4M allow you to group multiple perspective mutations into a single atomic transaction. This is useful when you need to perform multiple related changes that should either all succeed or all fail together, and when you want to optimize performance by reducing internal engine updates (query engine indexing, and Prolog inference if activated) and network operations.
data.1-atomicity#1. Atomicity:
All operations in a batch are applied together or none are applied
Prevents partial updates that could leave your data in an inconsistent state
Ideal for complex operations that require multiple related changes
data.2-performance-optimization#2. Performanc:
Reduces the number of internal engine updates (query engine indexing, query subscriptions, and Prolog inference if activated)
Minimizes the number of commits to the neighbourhood's link language
Batches network operations for shared perspectives
Improves overall system responsiveness when making multiple changes
data.batch-storage#Batch Storage:
Batches are stored in memory until committed
Each batch has a unique UUID
Changes are tracked separately for shared and local links
data.engine-synchronization#Engine Synchroniz:
Internal indexes (SPARQL store, query subscriptions, and Prolog facts if activated) are updated only once per batch commit
Updates are performed using a oneshot channel to ensure completion
The engine state remains consistent with all changes
data.link-language-integration#Link Language:
For shared perspectives, commits to the link language happen only once per batch
Reduces network operations in distributed scenarios
data.best-practices#Best Practices:
Prefer transaction(): Use Ad4mModel.transaction() over manual createBatch()/commitBatch() — if the callback throws, the batch is not committed and no changes are persisted.
Batch Size: Keep batches focused on related operations. Avoid extremely large batches that could impact memory usage — split very large operations into multiple smaller batches.
Error Handling: With transaction(), errors thrown inside the callback automatically prevent commit. With manual batches, wrap operations in try/catch.
Resource Management: Don't keep batches open longer than necessary. With transaction() this is handled for you.
Testing: Test both successful and failed batch scenarios. Verify data consistency after batch operations.
data.limitations-and-considerations#Limitatio:
Memory Usage
Batches store changes in memory until committed
Very large batches may impact system performance
Concurrency
Batch operations don't provide explicit locking
Consider application-level synchronization for concurrent operations
Network Connectivity
For shared perspectives, ensure stable network connectivity before committing large batches
Consider implementing retry logic for network-related failures

data:
ad4m-executor run can read its settings from a JSON file instead of flags,
so a headless executor (a systemd service, a container) keeps them in one
place and restarts with the same settings. The keys are the ones the ADAM
Launcher writes to ~/.ad4m/launcher-state.json.
ad4m-executor run --config /etc/ad4m/executor-config.json
# or
AD4M_CONFIG=/etc/ad4m/executor-config.json ad4m-executor run
There is no default path: without --config (or AD4M_CONFIG), run
behaves as before and uses only flags and environment variables.
data.precedence#Precedence:
Each setting is taken from the last of these that sets it:
the config file,
an AD4M_<FLAG> environment variable,
the flag.
ad4m-executor config print takes the same flags and prints the merged
result as JSON, with every secret replaced by "<redacted>" (an unset
secret shows as null):
ad4m-executor config print --config /etc/ad4m/executor-config.json --port 12400
data.keys#Keys:
Every key is optional. The file is rejected at startup if it contains a key
not listed here, at any depth (a typo fails loudly instead of being
ignored, and the error names the key by its path, e.g.
multi_user_config.tls_config.tls_prot), or a secret value (see
Secrets).
Key	Type	Default	Flag / variable	app_data_path	string	~/.ad4m	--app-data-path / AD4M_APP_DATA_PATH	port	number	12000	--port / AD4M_PORT	hc_admin_port	number	first free from 2000	--hc-admin-port / AD4M_HC_ADMIN_PORT	hc_app_port	number	first free from 1337	--hc-app-port / AD4M_HC_APP_PORT	localhost	bool	true	--localhost / AD4M_LOCALHOST	run_dapp_server	bool	true (port 8080)	--run-dapp-server / AD4M_RUN_DAPP_SERVER	auto_permit_cap_requests	bool	false with a config file, true without	--auto-permit-cap-requests / AD4M_AUTO_PERMIT_CAP_REQUESTS	mcp_enabled	bool	false	--enable-mcp / AD4M_ENABLE_MCP	mcp_port	number	3001	--mcp-port / AD4M_MCP_PORT	log_config	object: crate → level	see below	RUST_LOG overrides it	multi_user_config.enabled	bool	false	--enable-multi-user / AD4M_ENABLE_MULTI_USER	multi_user_config.tls_config	object or null	no TLS	see below	multi_user_config.smtp_config	object or null	no email	see below	
Inside the nested objects some keys are required: enabled in
multi_user_config; enabled, cert_file_path and key_file_path in
tls_config; every key but password_file in smtp_config.
tls_config and smtp_config may be null or left out.A string value that is empty or only whitespace ("app_data_path": "")
stops run with an error that names the key
(`app_data_path` is empty or only whitespace). Leave an optional key
out to get its default.multi_user_config.enabled: false (or --enable-multi-user false) does not
turn multi-user off on a data directory where it was enabled before: the
executor records multi-user as on in its database and only ever sets it.tls_config starts an HTTPS/WSS listener on 0.0.0.0:<tls_port>. The
plain RPC port then stays on 127.0.0.1.
{ "enabled": true, "cert_file_path": "/etc/ad4m/tls/cert.pem",
  "key_file_path": "/etc/ad4m/tls/key.pem", "tls_port": null }
tls_port: null means port + 1. The flags --tls-cert-file,
--tls-key-file and --tls-port (AD4M_TLS_CERT_FILE, AD4M_TLS_KEY_FILE,
AD4M_TLS_PORT) override the file's values; giving a certificate or key
flag turns TLS on, and TLS without both a certificate and a key stops run.smtp_config is the account multi-user verification emails are sent from.
{ "enabled": true, "host": "smtp.example.org", "port": 465,
  "username": "ad4m@example.org", "from_address": "ad4m@example.org",
  "password_file": "/etc/ad4m/secrets/smtp-password" }
With enabled: true, run stops unless a password is set (see
Secrets).log_config sets a level (error, warn, info, debug, trace)
per crate over the defaults rust_executor: info, holochain: warn,
wasmer_compiler_cranelift: warn, warp::server: info.Settings with no config key are flags only, each with its
AD4M_<FLAG> variable: --network-bootstrap-seed,
--language-language-only, --connect-holochain, --run-holochain,
--hc-use-bootstrap, --hc-use-local-proxy, --hc-use-mdns,
--hc-use-proxy, --hc-proxy-url, --hc-bootstrap-url, --hc-relay-url,
--log-holochain-metrics, --dynamic-class-tools, --pid-file,
--insecure-no-admin-credential.
The variable name is the flag in upper case with - as _, prefixed with
AD4M_: --hc-relay-url reads AD4M_HC_RELAY_URL.A variable that is set but empty or only whitespace stops run with an
error that names it (AD4M_APP_DATA_PATH is set but empty or only
whitespace), and so does such a flag value.
Neither is laid over the file: AD4M_APP_DATA_PATH=${DATA_DIR} with
DATA_DIR unset would otherwise put the data directory under the working
directory. Unset the variable to use the file's value.
data.secrets#Secrets:
The config file never holds a secret value. An admin_credential key or a
smtp_config.password key stops run with an error that names the key.
Secrets come from files or environment variables:
Secret	From a file	From a value	In the config file	Admin credential	AD4M_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL_FILE	AD4M_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL	—	SMTP password	AD4M_SMTP_PASSWORD_FILE	AD4M_SMTP_PASSWORD	smtp_config.password_file	Agent passphrase	AD4M_UNLOCK_PASSPHRASE_FILE	—	—	
Setting both variables of one secret stops run. The variables win over
smtp_config.password_file.
A secret file must not be readable by group or others: mode 0600 or
0400, otherwise run stops and names the file and its mode.
One trailing newline is removed, so echo "$SECRET" > file works.
An empty secret stops run: an empty file (or one holding only a
newline), an empty AD4M_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL or AD4M_SMTP_PASSWORD, or
--admin-credential "". An empty admin credential would match the empty
token a client without credentials sends.
--admin-credential <value> still works and wins over both variables,
but the value is visible to every user on the host through ps. Prefer
the file.
Neither run, config print nor the executor's log prints a secret
value, at any log level.
Under systemd, load the files with LoadCredential= and point the variables
at the credentials directory:
LoadCredential=admin-credential:/etc/ad4m/secrets/admin-credential
LoadCredential=unlock-passphrase:/etc/ad4m/secrets/unlock-passphrase
Environment=AD4M_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL_FILE=%d/admin-credential
Environment=AD4M_UNLOCK_PASSPHRASE_FILE=%d/unlock-passphrase
data.unlocking-at-startup#Unlocking at startu:
With AD4M_UNLOCK_PASSPHRASE_FILE set, the executor unlocks its agent
itself once it has started, as agent.unlock would, so a restarted node
serves requests without anyone unlocking it. It logs
Agent unlocked at startup on success. On a wrong passphrase it logs an
error starting Unlocking the agent at startup … failed, keeps running
with the agent locked, and waits for agent.unlock. If no agent has been
generated yet it logs a warning and does nothing; generate the agent, and
the next start unlocks it.
data.example#Example:
{
  "app_data_path": "/var/lib/ad4m",
  "port": 12400,
  "hc_admin_port": 12401,
  "hc_app_port": 12402,
  "run_dapp_server": false,
  "multi_user_config": {
    "enabled": true,
    "tls_config": null,
    "smtp_config": {
      "enabled": true, "host": "smtp.example.org", "port": 465,
      "username": "ad4m@example.org", "from_address": "ad4m@example.org",
      "password_file": "/etc/ad4m/secrets/smtp-password"
    }
  },
  "log_config": { "rust_executor": "info", "holochain": "warn" },
  "mcp_enabled": true,
  "mcp_port": 3003
}
AD4M_ADMIN_CREDENTIAL_FILE=/etc/ad4m/secrets/admin-credential \
AD4M_UNLOCK_PASSPHRASE_FILE=/etc/ad4m/secrets/unlock-passphrase \
  ad4m-executor run --config /etc/ad4m/executor-config.json

data: AD4M provides a set of React hooks to easily work with core AD4M concepts like Agents, Perspectives, and Subjects. These hooks handle state management, caching, and real-time updates automatically.
data.uselivequery#useLiveQuery: Provides reactive, live-updating access to AD4M model data with support for collections, single instances, pagination, and parent-scoped queries. Replaces the previous useModel hook.
data.return-types#Return Types:
Collection mode (LiveCollectionResult<T>):
data: T[] — Array of model instances
loading: boolean — Whether a query is in progress
error: string — Error message if any
totalCount: number — Total matching items (for pagination)
loadMore: () => void — Load next page
Single-instance mode (LiveInstanceResult<T>):
data: T | null — The model instance or null
loading: boolean
error: string
data.important-notes#Important Notes:
Registration: Call <ModelClass>.register(perspective) once at app startup (e.g., await Recipe.register(perspective)) — the hook does not register models automatically. Use the concrete generated class, not the @Model decorator.
Cleanup: Subscriptions are automatically disposed on component unmount.
String model support: You can pass a model class name string instead of a class for dynamic/generic use cases.

data: AD4M uses a high-performance SPARQL query engine powered by Oxigraph, executing entirely server-side in Rust. SPARQL gives you direct access to the RDF graph that underlies every Perspective, enabling powerful queries against link data, metadata, and relationships.
data.accessing-metadata#Accessing Metadata: The reifier pattern stores metadata on the link node itself. You can access author, timestamp, and other metadata:
data.graph-traversal#Graph Traversal: Single-hop traversal is just a basic filter — combine the source/target/predicate patterns shown above. SPARQL's real strength is chaining graph patterns to express multi-hop queries:
data.performance-notes#Performance Notes:
All SPARQL queries execute server-side in Rust via Oxigraph — no data is transferred to JS until results are ready
The Oxigraph store maintains indexes on subjects, predicates, and objects for fast lookups
Use specific patterns (filter on predicate, source, or target) rather than unbounded ?s ?p ?o for best performance
LIMIT and OFFSET are handled efficiently by the query engine
For paginated model data, prefer perspective.modelQuery() which combines SPARQL with server-side hydration
data.related-resources#Related Resources:
Model Classes Guide — Using Ad4mModel with the SPARQL engine
Perspectives — Understanding perspectives and links
Social DNA — Advanced query patterns with SDNA

/developer-guides/writing-a-flow.title: Writing a flow: a role granted by a flow

data:
This guide builds one thing, step by step: a task flow whose final edge only a reviewer can settle, where "reviewer" is not a label somebody typed but the output of a second flow the group ran. One flow gates on what another flow produced. That is the "fractal" case, and it is the most complex thing the flow engine does today.Every step is taken from tests/js/tests/model/flow-task-handover.test.ts. The code blocks are copied from that file, re-indented, and trimmed where noted. Read this page and you can rebuild Part 3 of that test without opening it. For what each API call means in general, see Flows; this page only repeats what the walkthrough needs.
  ReviewerRoleGrant flow                  TaskFlow (gated)
  ─────────────────────                   ────────────────
  subject: a ReviewerRole instance        subject: a Task
                                          Done needs n:1 vote from a DID that
  Proposed ──Grant (n:2)──▶ Granted       holds a ReviewerRole instance which
            names output:                 is a verified OUTPUT of a Granted
            (HandoverReviewerRole, role)  ReviewerRoleGrant run
                  │                                   ▲
                  │ mintFlowReceipt(run)              │
                  ▼                                   │
  handover://ReviewerRoleGrantFlow ──ad4m://flow/flow_receipt──▶ receipt
                  (the per-flow index the gate reads)
data.what-you-will-build#What you will build:
A four-state TaskFlow: Ready → InProgress → InReview → Done.
A Done edge gated by fromRole, so only a reviewer's vote counts.
A two-state ReviewerRoleGrant flow that runs over a role instance.
The hole: plain fromRole accepts the role instance before the grant flow has moved.
The fix: producedByFlow on the role query, which counts only a minted receipt of the grant.
The test uses two DIDs on one executor: Alice (a managed user) and Bob (the admin). They share one perspective. Everything below runs on that perspective.
data.the-whole-sequence#The whole sequence:
Alice                          graph                              Bob
  ─────                          ─────                              ───
  create ReviewerRole(bob) ────▶ role                    (nomination)
  start ReviewerRoleGrant ─────▶ run G [Proposed]
  create GrantEndorsement ─────▶ under role              (guard evidence)
  Grant, outputs=[role] ───────▶ proposal P (1/2)
                                 proposal P (2/2) ◀──── Grant, outputs=[role]
                                 run G derives Granted, settled_at = t1
  addFlow GatedTaskFlow ───────▶ Done: fromRole + producedByFlow(G, Granted)
  ... task to InReview ...
                                 vote on Done at t2 ◀── Accept
                                 gate: index of G is empty → Bob not a member
                                 run T stays InReview
  mintFlowReceipt(G) ──────────▶ receipt R; G ──flow_receipt──▶ R
                                 next derivation of T:
                                 R verifies, names (ReviewerRole, role),
                                 grant dated t1 < t2 → Bob's vote counts
                                 run T derives Done
data.what-each-replica-checks#What each repli:
This is the part that decides what a receipt of the gated task flow means to someone else. It is verified against the executor on this branch (rust-executor/src/perspectives/flow_instance/grant.rs, roles/mod.rs, read_set.rs).
Eligibility is decided inside the neighbourhood, per replica, against its own graph. While a replica collects the evidence for a derivation, it loads the granting flow's receipt index, verifies every receipt under its own flow catalogue, and computes, per matched role instance, the earliest settled_at of a verifying receipt that names it. That date is produced_at.
Only the date travels. The read-set carries produced_at for each role instance, next to the grant and revocation links. The granting receipt itself is not carried, and verifying a receipt of the gated flow never recurses into the granting flow's receipts.
There is no fallback. With producedByFlow on the role, an instance with no produced_at contributes no membership window at all. The assignment link's timestamp and the instance's own timestamp are never consulted. If they were, writing one link would grant the role and the gate would be decorative.
The rule comes from the reader's flow definition, never from the evidence. Which flow grants, and which class name binds, are read from the definition the verifying replica holds. A minter cannot name the rule its own receipt is judged by.
Cannot decide is an error, not "no". A granting flow this replica does not hold, or a receipt index over its budget, aborts the derivation of every flow gated on it. "I could not check" is neither "granted" nor "not granted".
So a receipt minted for a gated flow proves that n people signed and when. It does not, on its own, prove to a reader outside the neighbourhood that those people were eligible. The reader takes the carried produced_at on the same footing as the carried grant links. Referencing the granting receipt by hash, carrying it, and transitive verification are follow-up work in #1140.
data.what-can-go-wrong#What can go wrong:
Each of these maps to a row in Errors and limits on the Flows page.
You named Done from Ready. Error: `Done` is not reachable from `Ready`. Only render availableTransitions. The same error, with Done on both sides, is the probe in Step 7.
You pressed Grant before writing the endorsement. Error naming the unmet guard. Write the GrantEndorsement under the role instance first.
You left outputs empty on the Grant press. No error. The run settles, the receipt mints, and it names nothing. flowValidOutputs stays empty and the gate never counts the holder. Name the role instance.
You named outputs on Start or SubmitForReview. Refused: those states are not terminal.
Bob's press named different outputs than Alice's. Refused, neither joined nor twinned. Agree on the outputs, or reject the open proposal.
You forgot to mint. Nothing fires. A settled grant without a receipt does not grant. Call mintFlowReceipt after the grant settles.
You minted a run in Proposed. Error: no settled edge. Reach quorum on Grant first.
You wrote grantedByFlow, or misspelt the key. addFlow rejects and stores nothing; the error names the state and the key, e.g. unknown key `fromRole.grantedByFlow` (renamed to `producedByFlow` in #1076). A definition that arrived by sync with that rule is refused when read: the edge fires for nobody, and the executor log names the key.
You omitted state from producedByFlow. The rule does not decode and the edge is refused for everyone.
The replica does not hold ReviewerRoleGrant. Error, never an empty result. Sync the Social DNA first.
Someone flooded the grant flow's receipt index past 256 entries. Error: ReceiptBudgetExceeded. The gate refuses rather than truncates. Remove the junk links.
You gated with count: { max: 0 }. Refused outright. That would make every failed verification a reason to grant.
The executable form of this page is
tests/js/tests/model/flow-task-handover.test.ts.
Parts 1 and 2 are Steps 1 and 2. Part 3 is Steps 3 to 8, in order.

data.understanding-expressions#Understanding:
In AD4M's agent-centric paradigm, all data is treated as a claim or statement made by an agent. These claims are called "Expressions" – following the metaphor of Languages, they are what agents "express" through different protocols (Languages). While they could be seen as simple data objects, Expressions are fundamentally different because they:
Always include cryptographic proof of who created them
Are always created through a specific Language
Have globally unique addresses in AD4M's universal addressing scheme
data.global-addressing#Global Addressing:
Every Expression in AD4M has a unique address in the format:
<language_hash>://<expression_address>
This means:
The Language's hash identifies how to interpret/resolve the address
The expression_address is Language-specific (could be a CID, URL, hash, etc.)
The full address is globally unique and resolvable by any AD4M instance
data.retrieving-expressions#Retrieving Expres:
Any agent can retrieve an Expression using its address:
const expression = await ad4m.expression.get("QmSocialApp123://post789");
The retrieved Expression includes:
The original data
Who created it (author DID)
When it was created
Cryptographic proof of authenticity
data.expression-types#Expression Types:
While Expressions can contain any type of data, there are several common patterns:
Literal Expressions
Simple data types (strings, numbers, objects)
Encoded directly in the address, percent-encoded the same way as Literal.from(value).toUrl()
Example: literal:base64encoded-content
Content Expressions
Larger data objects (posts, documents, media)
Stored in a distributed system (IPFS, Holochain, etc.)
Example: QmSocialApp123://post789
Reference Expressions
Point to data in other systems
Act as bridges to existing protocols
Example: http://example.com/resource
data.expressions-and-trust#Expressions and Tr:
The agent-centric nature of Expressions enables a web of trust:
Authenticity: Every Expression is cryptographically signed, so you can verify who created it
Provenance: The timestamp and author create an audit trail
Context: Expressions can be referenced and linked in Perspectives, creating semantic meaning
Interoperability: Any AD4M instance can verify and interpret Expressions
data.best-practices#Best Practices:
When working with Expressions:
Choose the Right Language
Use literal Language for simple, small data
Use specialized Languages for specific data types
Consider storage requirements and accessibility
Handle Verification
Always check the proof.valid field
Consider the Expression's author in your trust model
Use timestamps for temporal context
Think Agent-Centric
Remember Expressions are claims made by agents
Consider how Expressions fit into social contexts
Use Perspectives to organize and give meaning to Expressions
For more details on implementing Languages that create and resolve Expressions, see the Language Development Guide.

/flows.title: Flows: State Machines a Group Agrees On

data.the-parts#The parts:
SHACLFlow  (the definition — Social DNA, shared as links)
  ├── FlowState        name, value, requires (guard), consensusRule
  └── FlowTransition   actionName, fromState → toState
        │
        │  FlowInstance.start(perspective, name, subjectUri)
        ▼
  FlowInstance  (one run, riding on a subject expression)
        │
        │  instance.proposeTransition(toState, rationale?, outputs?)
        ▼
  FlowTransitionProposal  (one proposed move; votes are signed links on it)
        │
        │  enough distinct eligible votes = the edge settles
        ▼
  derived state  (recomputed from the signed links, never stored)
        │
        │  terminal state reached → perspective.mintFlowReceipt(instanceUri)
        ▼
  FlowReceipt  (portable proof: this quorum settled this run into this state,
        │       and committed to these outputs)
        ▼
  consumers: perspective.flowValidOutputs, verifyFlowReceipt,
             model queries with where: { producedByFlow },
             role gates with fromRole.producedByFlow
data.the-one-rule#The one rule:
A flow's state is never stored. It is derived, every time, from the signed links present right now.To answer "what state is this task in?", the engine:
starts at the flow's lowest-valued state,
looks at the declared edges that leave it,
takes the edge that collected enough distinct, eligible signatures earliest,
repeats from the state that edge leads to,
stops at the first state where no edge has reached quorum. That state is the answer.
Three consequences, all intended:
Two replicas agree without talking. Same links in, same state out. Every choice in the walk is made by an explicit sort key, never by the order a database returned rows.
A third party can check the work. The derivation is a pure function over plain data. Hand someone the links and they can re-run it and reach your verdict.
Retracting a vote moves the flow back. Withdraw the signature that settled an edge and the flow stands where it stood before you signed. That is the semantics, not a bug. See Reject is not cancel.
The engine does write a currentState value onto each flow instance, but it
is a cache for readers, never authority. It is a Local link — it never
syncs — and nothing in the derivation reads it. Read it for display. Never
decide anything on it.
data.proposing-and-voting#Proposing and votin:
The button a UI puts on each availableTransitions entry calls proposeTransition. The executor evaluates the guard on this replica, seals the evidence, and either mints a proposal or co-signs the one another agent already opened for the same edge.
import { FlowInstance, type FlowProposeResult } from "@coasys/ad4m";
const result: FlowProposeResult = await instance.proposeTransition(
  "Done",
  "Deliverable present and reviewed.",
);
result.proposalUri;   // hand this to another agent, or to rejectProposal
result.minted;        // true = this call wrote the proposal
result.recordedVote;  // true = this DID's vote landed (mint or join)
result.outcomes;      // FlowFireOutcome[] — empty while short of quorum
result.derivedState;  // where the derivation stands after the call
result.contested;     // true = stalled; do not render "awaiting votes"
Read FlowProposeResult with this table. A bare outcome list cannot tell these cases apart:
outcomes	recordedVote	minted	meaning	non-empty	—	—	the transition fired	[]	true	true	you opened the proposal; waiting for other voters	[]	true	false	you joined someone else's proposal	[]	false	false	you had already voted; nothing was written	[]	—	—	plus contested: true: stalled, not waiting	
An empty outcome list is a normal answer. A vote short of quorum is a landed vote, not a failure.Two agents who want the same transition both press the same button. The second call finds the open proposal for that edge and co-signs it instead of minting a twin:
// Done has consensusRule { n: 2 }. Alice presses first:
const alicePress = await aliceInstance.proposeTransition("Done", "Deliverable present and reviewed.");
alicePress.outcomes;      // [] — one of two votes
alicePress.minted;        // true
alicePress.derivedState;  // "InReview" — unchanged
// Bob presses the SAME button on his view — not acceptProposal:
const bobPress = await bobInstance.proposeTransition("Done");
bobPress.outcomes[0].toState;  // "Done" — two distinct DIDs is quorum
bobPress.outcomes[0].voters;   // [aliceDid, bobDid]
bobPress.minted;               // false — he joined Alice's proposal
bobPress.proposalUri === alicePress.proposalUri; // true
From flow-task-handover.test.ts, Part 1.A vote on a listed proposal is also available directly: instance.acceptProposal(proposalUri) adds this DID's signature and re-derives. On the wire these calls are perspective.proposeFlowTransition, perspective.acceptFlowProposal and perspective.rejectFlowProposal, and over MCP the flow_proposal_accept / flow_proposal_reject tools.
data.quorum-belongs-to-the-edge#Quorum belong: When two replicas mint proposals for the same transition concurrently — each not yet having seen the other's — one edge carries twin proposals. If quorum were counted per proposal, a flow with n: 2 and two twins holding one vote each would sit at genesis forever, both one short. So the engine asks "did this edge collect n distinct voters?", across every proposal for it. Twins converge, and each appears in the outcome's contributingProposalUris.
data.contention#Contention: If two edges out of the current state both reach quorum, the engine does not pick a winner. It reports contention and the walk stops there. Choosing by timestamp would adjudicate a race with numbers the racing agents wrote themselves. A contested flow is stalled, not waiting: more votes cannot move it. While an instance is contested, proposeTransition into it is refused, and anything that pays out on a completed flow must refuse a contested derivation.
data.outputs-what-a-final-step-names#Outputs::
A run's outputs are the instances the group agrees the run produced — the deliverable a review accepted, the role a grant ceremony granted. The proposer of the final transition names them as (className, id) pairs:
// The grant flow's final press names the role instance as the run's output:
await grantInstance.proposeTransition("Granted", undefined, [
  { className: "HandoverReviewerRole", id: role.id },
]);
From flow-task-handover.test.ts, "Part 3 — grant flow over a ReviewerRole …".Rules, each enforced by the engine:
The run's subject is never an output by default. Name it, or the receipt speaks for nothing.
Outputs can only be named on a proposal into a terminal state. Naming them elsewhere is refused: the run does not end there.
Every named output must be an instance of its named class on the proposing replica, checked by the same rule every voter re-runs.
Every co-signer must name the same outputs. A press that names different outputs than the open proposal is refused, not joined — joining would sign outputs the presser did not name.
Why the content is hashed. The proposal signs outputs_hash, a digest over each output's (class, id, canonical content), next to the evidence seal. Every voter loads each named output through its class on their own graph, recomputes the hash, and refuses to co-sign on a mismatch. The receipt minted later must hash its carried outputs to that same quorum-signed commitment. Without the content in the hash, an id would be a movable target: any property of the instance could change after the vote while the id stayed the same, and the receipt would then speak for content the quorum never saw. "Content" here is exactly what a model query returns for the instance through its class: every scalar property, relations and collections as the ids they point at, and the synthetic createdAt / updatedAt / author fields.
data.producedbyflow-on-a-role-a-role-granted-:
Plain fromRole matches the instance. Adding producedByFlow to the role query adds the condition that the instance must be a valid output of a completed run of another flow. For a full walkthrough see Writing a flow: a role granted by a flow.
consensusRule: {
  n: 1,
  fromRole: {
    className: "HandoverReviewerRole",
    where: { domain: "frontend" },
    didProperty: "agent",
    producedByFlow: {
      flow: "handover://ReviewerRoleGrantFlow",  // `${namespace}${name}Flow`
      state: "Granted",
    },
  },
}
It is the same name and the same check as the producedByFlow model-query filter, with one difference: on a role, both fields are required. Without state, a run that settled into the flow's "rejected" state would grant what its "approved" state was meant to. A producedByFlow without state does not decode, and an undecodable rule refuses the edge rather than falling back to a default.
Spell the key exactly. A consensusRule with a key the engine does not
know — a misspelt key, or grantedByFlow, the name this gate had before it
was renamed — is refused, the same as a rule that does not decode. addFlow
refuses it up front: the call rejects with an error naming the state and
the key (for example unknown key `fromRole.grantedByFlow` (renamed to
  `producedByFlow` in #1076)), and nothing of the definition is stored. A
definition that reached the store another way — synced from a peer, or
written before this check existed — is refused when it is read: the edge it
governs fires for nobody, and the executor log names the key. The key is
never dropped, so the gate never falls back to plain fromRole
(#1144; flow-task-handover.test.ts
Part 4). This covers every object in the rule: the rule itself, fromRole
and its or arms, count, producedByFlow, an object linkedTo, and
each object-valued where condition. It does not cover requires guards or
context, which still ignore unknown keys.
A key written twice anywhere in the rule (possible in a hand-written JSON
literal) is refused the same way; the last one does not win.
For each candidate instance, the gate asks whether a receipt under the granting flow's index verifies against this replica's own flow definitions, was minted for that flow, settled into state — the state the replica's own re-fold derives, not the one the receipt asserts — and names the instance by (className, id) among its outputs. The className is the one in your fromRole query, read from your own flow definition, never from anything the receipt or the carried evidence says. A node committed as a Task is not a produced HandoverReviewerRole, even with the same id.The grant is dated from the receipt's settled_at — the moment the n-th distinct eligible voter signed the grant's final edge. When several receipts name the instance, the earliest wins. No participant picks that time, and there is no fallback to the assignment link or the instance's own timestamp: if there were, writing one link would grant the role and the gate would be decorative.The full loop, from a UI, in three calls:
// 1. The Grant presses name the role instance as the run's output.
//    Every co-signer names the same outputs.
await grant.proposeTransition("Granted", undefined, [
  { className: "HandoverReviewerRole", id: role.id },
]);
// (a second member presses the same button to reach the grant's n:2)
// 2. Once the run has settled, any member mints its receipt:
await perspective.mintFlowReceipt(grantRunUri);
// 3. Optional — inspect what the gate will read:
await perspective.flowValidOutputs("handover://ReviewerRoleGrantFlow", "Granted");
From flow-task-handover.test.ts, Part 3.The gate is fail-closed, and Part 3 pins each direction:
A settled grant run without a minted receipt does not grant. Bob's vote on the gated task did not count until someone called mintFlowReceipt. "The run completed" is not evidence. A receipt is.
Once the receipt exists, votes cast before the mint count on the next derivation — the vote was always valid, the gate just could not verify the grant yet. Nothing new needs to be written.
The receipt is bound to its instance by (className, id). Alice's own role instance — same class, same domain — did not pass the gate, because no receipt names her instance. A receipt is never "flow F completed"; it is "flow F produced this".
Where the check runs, and what travels. Each replica decides eligibility against its own graph, while it collects the evidence for a fold. The read-set then carries only the result: for each matched role instance, the grant date (produced_at, the granting run's settled_at). The granting receipt itself does not travel, and verifying a receipt never recurses into the granting flow's receipts.So a receipt minted for a gated flow proves that n people signed, and when. It does not, on its own, prove to a reader outside the neighbourhood that those people were allowed to sign: the minting replica decided that against its graph, and the verifier re-folds with the carried grant dates and trusts them, the same way it trusts that the carried grant links were all the links there were. Referencing the granting receipt by hash, optionally carrying it, and transitive verification are future work (#1140).The gate has three outcomes, not two:
Granted. A verified receipt names this instance.
Not granted. No verified receipt names it. The instance contributes nothing, exactly as if the role query had not matched it.
Cannot decide. The replica does not hold the granting flow, or the flow's receipt index is over budget. This comes back as an error, and the flow whose rule asked cannot derive a state until it is resolved. The error means "unknown", not "no".
Do not write if (granted) allow else deny around a call that can throw. If you catch the error and deny, you bring back the silent denial that the engine refuses to give: a flood of junk index links would then deny every holder, with no signal. Show the error, or retry after sync. "Fail-closed" above means that an unproven grant never counts. It does not mean that an undecidable gate reads as "not a member".Un-granting is the normal role revocation: a signed tombstone on the role instance. It stops future votes. It does not invalidate the receipt, and undoing the granting flow does not un-grant either: retracting a settling vote moves the live flow back, while the minted receipt keeps verifying. Who may write that tombstone follows the role query's where.author — absent: anyone; "$did": only the holder; a specific DID: only that DID, and if it is unreachable, the grant is permanent. There is no way to make a producedByFlow grant expire.One shape is refused outright: producedByFlow together with a count that zero instances satisfy, such as { max: 0 }. That would read "eligible while no verified receipt exists", so every reason a receipt fails to verify would become a reason to grant.
data.errors-and-limits#Errors and limits:
The refusals a developer will meet, what each one means, and what to do:
You did	You get	It means	Do	proposeTransition("Done") from a state with no declared edge to Done	error naming the states, e.g. `Done` is not reachable from `Ready`	the flow's transitions do not include this edge from the derived state (not the cache)	render only availableTransitions; re-read derivedState from the error	proposeTransition into a state whose requires is unmet	error naming the unmet guard	the guard query found no match on this replica at mint time	write the evidence first, or wait for it to sync	proposeTransition while the instance is contested	refusal	two edges out of the current state both hold quorum; the group must resolve it socially (retract votes)	do not retry; surface the contention	proposeTransition with outputs into a non-terminal state	refusal	a run does not end there, so there is nothing the outputs could be outputs of	name outputs only on the final transition	proposeTransition with outputs different from the open proposal's	refusal (neither joined nor twinned)	co-signing would sign outputs you did not name; a twin would split the final edge's commitment	co-sign or reject the open proposal, or agree on the outputs	rejectProposal on a proposal you never signed	error	there is nothing of yours to withdraw; a link that merely names your DID is not yours	nothing — only signers can retract	mintFlowReceipt on a run that has not settled	error: no settled edge	the fold found no completed final transition, so there is nothing to freeze	reach quorum on the final transition first	flowValidOutputs / the producedByFlow filter / a fromRole with producedByFlow naming a flow this replica does not hold	error, never []	"I cannot check" must not read as "there are none"	sync the flow definition (the Social DNA) first	a query or role gate on a flow whose receipt index holds more than 256 candidates	error: ReceiptBudgetExceeded	anyone can write index links, so over the budget the read refuses rather than truncates — a truncated read could hide the one genuine receipt	remove the junk links from the flow's receipt index; the error names the flow and the count	a fromRole with producedByFlow and a count satisfied by zero (e.g. { max: 0 })	error: refusing to gate	a receipt that fails to verify would make the voter eligible, not ineligible	drop the count, or gate on a positive count	a fromRole with producedByFlow but no state	the rule does not decode; the edge is refused	a grant without a named state would also be granted by a run that settled into "rejected"	name the state the granting run must settle into	a consensusRule with a key the engine does not know (e.g. grantedByFlow, formRole, count: { mxa }), or a key written twice	addFlow rejects and stores nothing, naming the state and the key; a definition that arrived by sync is refused when read: the edge fires for nobody and the executor log names the key	a dropped key would widen the gate or remove it	fix the key named in the error	a malformed producedByFlow filter (wrong shape, or nested inside OR/AND/NOT)	error	a filter that cannot be read must not admit everything	fix the filter shape: { flow, state? } at the top level of where	
Limits that are absences, not errors — do not go looking for these:
No flow subscriptions. There is no onStateChange or onProposalAdded. Poll FlowInstance.findAll, proposals(), or the currentStateName cache.
No read that re-derives without voting. currentStateName is the engine's cache. The calls that re-derive are the ones that act (proposeTransition, acceptProposal); their derivedState and their refusal messages name the derived state.
No automatic receipt minting. A settled run gets a receipt only when someone calls mintFlowReceipt.
No direct fire. An edge fires only by reaching quorum. FlowTransition.actions is declared and not executed.
data.guarantees-and-non-guarantees#Guarantees:
Each claim below is enforced by a named code branch in rust-executor/src/perspectives/flow_instance/, and tested where a test is named.The engine guarantees:
Determinism. Two replicas holding the same links derive the same state. Every choice in the fold is made by an explicit sort key (fold.rs; the fold is a pure function with no I/O).
Only self-signed facts count. Every field of a proposal is read only from links the proposer signed, with the executor's signature verdict valid (atom.rs, signed_by, unique_field). A synced link claiming to be part of a proposal but signed by someone else is invisible. A proposer who published two values for one field invalidates their own proposal. There is no last-write-wins on this path.
A vote binds the proposal's content. The proposal URI is the content address of its signed fields — instance, edge, evidence seal, outputs commitment — recomputed on every read (atom.rs, proposal_uri). A vote signs that URI, so neither a peer nor the proposer can re-point a voted proposal's fields afterwards.
Quorum cannot be manufactured by timestamps. Quorum is a count of distinct eligible DIDs (fold.rs, settle_edge). Back-dating a vote can shift when an edge settled, never whether it settled.
Eligibility is judged as of each vote's own timestamp (roles.rs; tested by flow-task-handover.test.ts Part 2). Revocation stops future votes and never un-settles history.
A co-sign re-checks the evidence and the outputs on the voter's own graph before signing, and refuses on any mismatch (accept.rs, check_outputs_commitment; Rust e2e ).
A receipt's outputs are what the quorum committed to. Mint refuses outputs that do not hash to the final edge's signed commitment, and verification re-hashes the carried preimages against it (receipt.rs, final_edge_commitment; verify.rs step 7; tested by the tampered-receipt case in flow-produced-by.test.ts, and Rust e2e ).
Every receipt consumer fails closed (produced.rs): only a Verified verdict counts, Undecidable is excluded, an unknown flow and an over-budget receipt index are errors, never empty answers (Rust e2e an_unknown_flow_is_an_error_not_an_empty_answer, a_receipt_flood_is_an_error_not_an_empty_answer).
A producedByFlow role gate has no fallback to the assignment link, binds by (className, id) with the class from the reader's own query, and dates the grant from the quorum's settled_at (grant.rs, roles/evidence.rs RoleGrantEvidence::resolve; tested by flow-task-handover.test.ts Part 3, both halves, and Rust e2e ).
The engine does NOT guarantee:
That any voter actually ran the checks before signing. The protocol requires each voter to recompute the seal and the outputs commitment and refuse on mismatch, and an honest client does. But the recomputation is not itself signed or carried, so a voter running modified code is indistinguishable from an honest one (verify.rs, the "not proven" table). The trust root of a receipt is the voter quorum, not the software.
That outputs still have the committed content now. A receipt attests to content at completion. The live-content check exists only on flowValidOutputs and the producedByFlow filter, not on verifyFlowReceipt and not on the grant gate — a grant keeps being honoured after the role instance accrues links.
That the voters on a gated flow were eligible, to a reader outside the neighbourhood. A producedByFlow gate is decided by each replica against its own graph, and the read-set carries only the resulting grant date, not the granting receipt. A receipt for a gated flow is verified with those carried dates taken on trust (grant.rs, § What a receipt of a gated flow proves; carrying the granting receipt is #1140).
Who authored the evidence or the instance. Instance authorship is never checked and never carried. Guard evidence is hashed, not author-verified.
A trustworthy settlement time for the first edge. Later edges settle no earlier than the walk's arrival at their from-state, but nothing bounds the first edge's timestamp backward: a genesis vote back-dated to 1970 settles at 1970 (fold.rs, § Ordering and time). Quorum is unaffected. Do not build anything that pays out on the settlement time of a flow's first edge.
Delivery or liveness. The engine derives over the links a replica holds. It does not guarantee that links sync, or when.

data.returns-35#Returns:
Promise<string>Complete SPARQL query string ready for executionDescriptionThis method translates high-level query parameters into a SPARQL query string
that can be executed against the SPARQL backend. Unlike Prolog queries which
operate on SDNA-aware predicates, SPARQL queries operate directly on raw links
stored in SPARQL.The generated query uses a CTE (Common Table Expression) pattern:
First, identify candidate base expressions by filtering links based on where conditions
Then, for each candidate base, resolve properties and relations via subqueries
Finally, apply ordering, pagination (LIMIT/START) at the SQL level
Key architectural notes:
SPARQL stores only raw links (source, predicate, target, author, timestamp)
No SDNA knowledge at the database level
Properties are resolved via subqueries that look for links with specific predicates
Relations are similar but return multiple values instead of one
Special fields (base, author, timestamp) are accessed directly, not via subqueries
Example
const query = Recipe.queryToSPARQL(perspective, {
  where: { name: "Pasta", rating: { gt: 4 } },
  order: { timestamp: "DESC" },
  limit: 10
});
// Returns: SELECT source AS base, array::first(target[WHERE predicate = ...]) AS name, ...
//          FROM link WHERE ... GROUP BY source ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10

@coasys/ad4m / Exports / AgentAD4M's representation of an AgentAD4M Agents are build around DIDs, which are used to identify and authenticate the Agent.
Conceptually, an Agent is regarded as something that can speak and that can listen.Agents speak by creating Expressions in AD4M Languages which are signed by the Agent's DID key,
And they also speak (broadcast) by putting semantic statements into their public "Agent Perspective".
They listen (can receive messages) through their "direct message Language".These three aspects are represented by the three fields of this class.This class is used as format for the Expressions in the Agent language.
Since AD4M treats DID URIs as addresses for the Agent Language,
DIDs are resolved to Expressions that are objects of this class.
Thus, this is how agents see (other) agents.

data.returns-23#Returns:
Promise<string>Complete SPARQL query string ready for executionDescriptionThis method translates high-level query parameters into a SPARQL query string
that can be executed against the SPARQL backend. Unlike Prolog queries which
operate on SDNA-aware predicates, SPARQL queries operate directly on raw links
stored in SPARQL.The generated query uses a CTE (Common Table Expression) pattern:
First, identify candidate base expressions by filtering links based on where conditions
Then, for each candidate base, resolve properties and relations via subqueries
Finally, apply ordering, pagination (LIMIT/START) at the SQL level
Key architectural notes:
SPARQL stores only raw links (source, predicate, target, author, timestamp)
No SDNA knowledge at the database level
Properties are resolved via subqueries that look for links with specific predicates
Relations are similar but return multiple values instead of one
Special fields (base, author, timestamp) are accessed directly, not via subqueries
Example
const query = Recipe.queryToSPARQL(perspective, {
  where: { name: "Pasta", rating: { gt: 4 } },
  order: { timestamp: "DESC" },
  limit: 10
});
// Returns: SELECT source AS base, array::first(target[WHERE predicate = ...]) AS name, ...
//          FROM link WHERE ... GROUP BY source ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10

▸ proposals(): Promise<FlowTransitionProposal[]>All FlowTransitionProposal records targeting this instance's URI.Uses the SDNA identity discriminator (ad4m://flow/instance predicate)
for the where-filter — one SPARQL round-trip, no client-side
filtering.These are written by the executor's consensus pass when it mints a

not swept here — a stale one is simply never counted by the fold, and

data.proposetransition#proposeTransition:
▸ proposeTransition(toState, rationale?, outputs?): Promise<FlowProposeResult>Propose a flow transition for this instance, as the calling agent.The executor evaluates the guard on its own replica, seals the evidence,
and either writes a new proposal or — when an equivalent one is already
open, i.e. another agent pressed the same button first — co-signs that
one. When the resulting vote reaches the target state's
consensusRule.n, the transition fires in the same call.How to read the result — fired vs. queued vs. no-op vs. stalled — is
documented on FlowProposeResult itself.outputs names the instances the run produces, as { className, id }
pairs, for a transition into a terminal state. The proposal signs a hash
over their content, every co-signer recomputes it on its own replica,
and a receipt for the run speaks for exactly these instances as they
stood at completion.Throws when toState is not reachable from the derived state, when the
target state carries a requires guard that is not currently satisfied
on this replica, when the instance is already contested, when outputs
is given for a non-terminal state or names something that is not an
instance of its class, or
when an open proposal on the same edge names different outputs.

data.findall#findAll:
▸ Static findAll(perspective, filter?): Promise<FlowInstance[]>Return every live FlowInstance on the perspective (design doc §4.3).Read-only path: never registers classes. On a perspective that has
never minted a flow instance, the FlowInstanceRecord SHACL shape
isn't installed yet — this returns [] in that case rather than
mutating the perspective. Registration is the responsibility of
start, which is the write path. (Registering on
a read would sync a write to every peer in the neighbourhood —
exactly what a query must not do — James PR #929 R7.)Filter surface (all optional, all combinable):
flowName — narrows by flow-name discriminator (e.g. "Delivery")
subject — narrows by base-expression URI, i.e. "give me every
flow running on THIS expression"
Both filters translate to a single SHACL where-filter round-trip
(no client-side filtering); combining them AND-joins server-side.
The string-arg shape (FlowInstance.findAll(p, "Delivery")) is
shorthand for { flowName: "Delivery" }.Records whose flow value has no matching SHACLFlow on the
perspective (e.g. the flow was unregistered) are silently skipped —
the wrapper can't answer currentState / availableTransitions
without the shape, and callers routinely iterate the returned array
without null-checks.

shape matches the Rust-side hardwired SDNA (parity-locked in

on-graph record, so currentState / availableTransitions /

data.acceptedby#acceptedBy:
• acceptedBy: string[] = []DIDs that accepted this proposal, as the consensus engine counts them:
an ad4m://acceptedBy link counts only when it is signed by the DID it
names, since anyone can write one naming someone else, and each DID once.
The proposer's vote is implicit and the proposer may also accept, so the
voters are the set { proposer } ∪ acceptedBy, not its sum.
Read-only: vote with acceptProposal, withdraw with rejectProposal.
data.evidence#evidence:
• evidence: string[] = []URIs of instances offered as evidence that toState.requires is now
satisfied. Multiple links, one per cited instance; ordering is not
significant.
data.evidencehashes#evidenceHashes:
• evidenceHashes: string = ""JSON blob: { [uri]: sha256_hex } — one entry per evidence URI, hashing
the canonicalized graph-visible properties (sorted by property URI,
multi-values sorted lexicographically) at proposal time. Downstream
verifiers use it to detect edits to cited instances after the proposal
was written. Stored as an opaque string because SHACL properties carry
no rich-object type; the engine parses it back into a map.
data.flowinstance#flowInstance:
• flowInstance: string = ""URI of the running FlowInstance this proposal targets. First-declared
property so buildSHACL derives the shape namespace from its through
prefix — ad4m://flow/instance → ad4m:// → target_class
ad4m://FlowTransitionProposal. Also the identity predicate: the
discriminator findAll uses to isolate proposal nodes.
data.fromstate#fromState: • fromState: string = ""Name of the state the flow instance is currently in.
data.nonce#nonce:
• nonce: string = ""The proposer's uniqueness salt for this proposal's content-addressed
URI (ad4m://flow/proposal/<hash>; the hash covers the instance, the
edge, the seal, the outputs commitment, the proposer DID and this
nonce). The engine writes a UUID. A proposal without one — or whose URI
does not match its own signed fields — is not engine-visible:
co-signatures name the URI, so the URI must commit to what they sign
(#1108).
data.outputs#outputs:
• outputs: string[] = []The instances the proposer names as the run's outputs. Written only on
a proposal into a terminal state; one link per output, ordering not
significant. Each entry is the canonical JSON text of a
{ className, id } pair (FlowOutputRef); JSON.parse it to read one.
data.outputshash#outputsHash:
• outputsHash: string = ""SHA-256 (hex) over the named outputs' content (each instance as
model_query returns it through its class), signed by the proposer
next to the evidence seal. Co-signers load the outputs and recompute it
before voting, and a flow receipt's output preimages must hash to it.
Empty on a proposal into a non-terminal state.
data.proposer#proposer:
• proposer: string = ""DID of the agent that issued the proposal, read the way the engine reads
it: only from a proposer link signed by the DID it names. Any member
can write a proposer link naming someone else, and an unchecked read
would show that DID instead (and drop the real proposer from the voters).
data.rationale#rationale:
• Optional rationale: stringFree-form human-readable justification. Optional — the LLM includes it
when it wants to explain why the cited evidence satisfies the state's
requires; the UI shows it to reviewers.
data.resolvedas#resolvedAs:
• Optional resolvedAs: string"fired" once this replica's consensus pass has recorded the transition
this proposal settled. Per-replica bookkeeping, never an input to the
engine's own derivation. Only this replica's own Local mark is read:
a Shared one a peer wrote says nothing about what happened here.
Read-only.

data.returns-23#Returns:
Promise<string>Complete SPARQL query string ready for executionDescriptionThis method translates high-level query parameters into a SPARQL query string
that can be executed against the SPARQL backend. Unlike Prolog queries which
operate on SDNA-aware predicates, SPARQL queries operate directly on raw links
stored in SPARQL.The generated query uses a CTE (Common Table Expression) pattern:
First, identify candidate base expressions by filtering links based on where conditions
Then, for each candidate base, resolve properties and relations via subqueries
Finally, apply ordering, pagination (LIMIT/START) at the SQL level
Key architectural notes:
SPARQL stores only raw links (source, predicate, target, author, timestamp)
No SDNA knowledge at the database level
Properties are resolved via subqueries that look for links with specific predicates
Relations are similar but return multiple values instead of one
Special fields (base, author, timestamp) are accessed directly, not via subqueries
Example
const query = Recipe.queryToSPARQL(perspective, {
  where: { name: "Pasta", rating: { gt: 4 } },
  order: { timestamp: "DESC" },
  limit: 10
});
// Returns: SELECT source AS base, array::first(target[WHERE predicate = ...]) AS name, ...
//          FROM link WHERE ... GROUP BY source ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10

data.returns-23#Returns:
Promise<string>Complete SPARQL query string ready for executionDescriptionThis method translates high-level query parameters into a SPARQL query string
that can be executed against the SPARQL backend. Unlike Prolog queries which
operate on SDNA-aware predicates, SPARQL queries operate directly on raw links
stored in SPARQL.The generated query uses a CTE (Common Table Expression) pattern:
First, identify candidate base expressions by filtering links based on where conditions
Then, for each candidate base, resolve properties and relations via subqueries
Finally, apply ordering, pagination (LIMIT/START) at the SQL level
Key architectural notes:
SPARQL stores only raw links (source, predicate, target, author, timestamp)
No SDNA knowledge at the database level
Properties are resolved via subqueries that look for links with specific predicates
Relations are similar but return multiple values instead of one
Special fields (base, author, timestamp) are accessed directly, not via subqueries
Example
const query = Recipe.queryToSPARQL(perspective, {
  where: { name: "Pasta", rating: { gt: 4 } },
  order: { timestamp: "DESC" },
  limit: 10
});
// Returns: SELECT source AS base, array::first(target[WHERE predicate = ...]) AS name, ...
//          FROM link WHERE ... GROUP BY source ORDER BY timestamp DESC LIMIT 10

data.dispose#dispose:
▸ dispose(): Promise<void>Disposes of the current subscription if one exists.This method:
Stops the keepalive signals to the subscription
Unsubscribes from subscription updates
Notifies the backend to clean up subscription resources
Clears the subscription reference
Steps 1, 2 and 4 happen synchronously, so builder.dispose() without
await is still a complete local cleanup. The returned promise resolves
once the executor has released this subscriber's hold on the subscription
(it never rejects). The executor shares one subscription between all
subscribers of the same query and only drops it when the last one
disposes, so disposing here does not interrupt another builder's updates.You should call this method when you're done with a subscription
to prevent memory leaks and ensure proper cleanup.

▸ parent(idOrInstance, modelOrPredicate?, options?): ModelQueryBuilder<T>Scopes the query to instances linked from a parent.The predicate is resolved in order of precedence:
Instance only — the parent's constructor is used as the model

has multiple relations targeting the same child class).
String id + model class — same metadata scan (or field lookup if

Passing a plain string id with no second argument throws because the
predicate cannot be resolved without a model class.

▸ Private #deliverResult(result): voidDeliver a result to consumers: complete a still-pending

▸ Private #releaseHold(): voidRelease this proxy's hold on its executor subscription, at most once.The executor hands every subscriber of the same query the same
subscription id and removes the entry when the last holder releases
it. The id is cleared before the RPC, so a repeated dispose() is a
local no-op and cannot release another subscriber's hold.
data.startkeepalive##startKeepalive:
▸ Private #startKeepalive(generation): voidStart the keepalive loop for the given generation. The loop runs
every 30s until it is superseded (generation mismatch — a newer
subscribe() or reconnect swap took over) or the proxy is disposed.
On a keepalive error it falls back to a full subscribe().
data.dispose#dispose:
▸ dispose(): voidClean up the subscription and stop keepalive signalsThis method:
Stops the keepalive timer
Unsubscribes from subscription updates
Clears all registered callbacks
Cleans up any pending initialization timeout
After calling this method, the subscription is no longer active and
will not receive any more updates. The instance should be discarded.
Calling it again is a no-op: subscribers of the same query share one
executor subscription, and only the first call releases this proxy's
hold on it.

▸ availableFlows(exprAddr): Promise<string[]>Returns all Social DNA flows that can be started from the given expression.Post-flowable retirement: a flow is a candidate iff its inputTypes
declaration is compatible with the expression. Matching rules:
Empty inputTypes or one containing the "any" wildcard → always
matches (same behaviour as the legacy flowable === "any" case).
Otherwise, at least one of the expression's registered subject-class
URIs (resolved via subjectClassesOf) must appear in
inputTypes. This is the concrete-type match the design doc's §5
spawn engine calls for; without it, a flow declaring
inputTypes: ["Task"] was previously never returned by
availableFlows("some-task-uri") — the entire point of typed
flows was silently unreachable (James PR #929 J#3).
The expression is classified against the perspective's registered
classes only. An expression whose class is not registered on this
perspective matches no typed flow (absence, not falsehood — same
discipline as subjectClassesOf); typed flows requiring
unknown classes are still returned to their untyped-caller peers.

▸ executeAction(actions, expression, parameters, batchId?): Promise<boolean>Executes a set of actions on an expression with optional parameters.
Used internally by Social DNA flows and subject class operations.Actions are specified as an array of commands that modify links in the perspective.
Each action is an object with the following format:
{
  action: "addLink" | "removeLink" | "setSingleTarget" | "collectionSetter",
  source: string,    // Usually "this" to reference the current expression
  predicate: string, // The predicate URI
  target: string     // The target value or "value" for parameters
}
Available commands:
addLink: Creates a new link
removeLink: Removes an existing link
setSingleTarget: Removes all existing links with the same source/predicate and adds a new one
collectionSetter: Special command for setting relation properties
When used with parameters, the special value "value" in the target field will be
replaced with the actual parameter value.

data.subjectclassesof#subjectClassesOf:
▸ subjectClassesOf(uris): Promise<Record<string, string[]>>Resolve each URI to the names of every subject class it is an instance of.The counterpart of isSubjectInstance, which asks the same question
one class at a time. Without this, finding the class of an arbitrary URI
meant looping over every registered class — a round trip each — and doing
it again for every URI.Class membership in AD4M is structural — a URI belongs to a class when it
carries that class's flags and required properties — so membership is not
exclusive: an instance conforms to its parent classes, and to any
unrelated class whose required set happens to be a subset of what it
carries. Every match is returned.The list is ordered most specific first, meaning by the number of
triples the class requires — a subclass requires everything its parent does
and more — with ties broken alphabetically so that every peer answers
identically. A caller that can only act on one class should take
classes[0], but that head is only a heuristic: it is arbitrary between two
unrelated classes requiring the same number of triples, which is exactly
the case the full list exists to expose.A URI is absent from the result when no registered class matched it.
That covers two situations, and nothing here separates them: the URI may
not be a subject instance at all, or it may be an instance of a class this
perspective has not registered. Absence is used rather than an empty list
because an empty list would claim the stronger thing — that the URI belongs
to no class — which this cannot know.

data.datatype#datatype:
• Optional datatype: stringExplicit SHACL sh:datatype for the property value. When set, this
overrides auto-inference and — importantly — lets custom getter
properties opt into typed-literal decoding. Auto-inference is disabled
for properties with a getter (see shacl-gen.ts) because such
getters typically return URIs; setting datatype explicitly declares
that this getter returns literal values of the given XSD type
(e.g. "xsd://string") and enables the hydration decode gate.
data.getter#getter:
• Optional getter: stringCustom getter to resolve the property value. Use this for custom graph traversals.
The expression can reference 'Base' which will be replaced with the instance's base expression.
Example: "SELECT ?target WHERE {  flux://has_reply ?target . } LIMIT 1"
data.identity#identity:
• Optional identity: booleanMarks this property as the class's identity (dedup key) for the
generic LLM interpreter: on re-runs, two proposed instances of the same
class with an equal (normalized/semantic) value on the identity property
are treated as the same instance rather than duplicated. Emitted as an
ad4m://identity link on the property shape and read back by the Rust
model query (ShapeProperty.identity). At most one property per class
should set this.
data.initial#initial: • Optional initial: stringThe initial value of the property. Required if the property is marked as required.
data.interpretationhint#interpretationHint:
• Optional interpretationHint: stringNatural-language hint that steers the generic LLM extractor when
turning a transcript into typed subject-class instances.  Emitted as
an ad4m://interpretation_hint link on the property shape and surfaced
on ShapeProperty.interpretation_hint by the Rust model query so the
extractor prompt can quote it verbatim.
data.local#local: • Optional local: booleanIndicates whether the property is stored locally in the perspective and not in the network. Useful for properties that are not meant to be shared with the network.
data.prologgetter#prologGetter: • Optional prologGetter: stringCustom Prolog getter to get the value of the property. If not provided, the default getter will be used.
data.prologsetter#prologSetter: • Optional prologSetter: stringCustom Prolog setter to set the value of the property. Only available if the property is writable.
data.readonly#readOnly:
• Optional readOnly: booleanIndicates whether the property is read-only. If true, no setter will be generated.
Defaults to false (property is writable).
data.required#required: • Optional required: booleanIndicates whether the property is required. If true, an initial value must be provided.
data.resolvelanguage#resolveLanguage:
• Optional resolveLanguage: stringThe language used to resolve/store the property value — and the sole
selector of storage mode. Not defaulted:
unset (the default for a plain @Property()) → deterministic
typed literal storage (literal:string: / :number: / :boolean: /

expression_create, producing a signed-envelope URI with
